topics.title: The boxing system & frame measurements
topics.summary: Frames and lenses are described with the boxing system: the smallest rectangle around each lens shape. Dr Hallam's facial measurement lecture uses it for every fitting measurement (heights from the HCL, centration from the box centre), and the numbers on the frame side give you the box size, DBL and side length.
keyPoints: DBL (distance between lenses): the horizontal distance between the nasal vertical sides of the two boxes around the lens shapes (British Standard definition).
HCL (horizontal centre line): the line halfway between the top and bottom horizontal tangents of the boxed lens.
A frame marked x□y zzz has horizontal boxed lens size x, DBL y and side length zzz.

Box centre distance = horizontal box size + DBL. If the patient's PD equals it, the optical centres sit in the middle of each box and the lenses can be thinnest (e.g. knife-edge on both sides in the aspherics worksheet).

Segment and fitting heights are given relative to the HCL (British Standard), always stating above or below. In practice progressives are often measured from the lowest point of the frame, so check which convention you're using.

For custom frames, the Fairbanks facial measurement rule gives the face's equivalents: PD, apical radius, head and temple width, bridge projection and height, splay and frontal angles, and DBR at 10 and 15 mm below the crest.
examTraps: Measuring DBL at the narrowest point of the bridge instead of between the boxes.
Giving a segment or fitting height without saying whether it's above or below the HCL.
Forgetting that a poor match between frame box centres and PD increases decentration, blank size and thickness.

diagram.description: Front view of a pair of lens shapes, each enclosed in a dashed rectangle. Label A across the top of the right box, B down its side, DBL between the boxes, the box centre (×) in each, the horizontal centre line joining them and BCD from × to ×.

goDeeper.heading: Why frame choice changes lens thickness
goDeeper.body: In the aspheric worksheet a +8.00 lens in a 50□20 frame for a 60 mm PD needed a 4.83 mm centre to be knife-edge temporally, because the optical centre was 5 mm in from the box centre. With a 70 mm PD (matching the box centres) the same lens needed only 3.44 mm. Smaller, rounder frames that match the PD keep plus lenses thin.

goDeeper.heading: Not in the slides: effective diameter and blank size
goDeeper.body: Effective diameter (ED) is twice the longest radius from the box centre to the lens edge, and minimum blank size is roughly ED + 2 × decentration + an edging allowance. Check your department's allowance.

topics.title: Facial measurements: PD, heights & vertex distance
topics.summary: Facial measurements put the optical centres, segments and fitting crosses where the eyes look. Dr Hallam's week 11 lecture covers how to measure distance and mono PDs, near centration distance, heights for multifocals and progressives, back vertex distance, and the pantoscopic and dihedral angles that free-form lenses need.
keyPoints: Wrong centration induces unwanted prism, causing discomfort or diplopia. Measure square-on, with your eyes level with the patient's, keeping both heads and the ruler still.

Distance PD with a ruler at arm's length: ruler on the nose, patient looks at your left eye while you set zero on their right pupil, then at your right eye while you read the left. At 40 cm each 1 mm difference between your PD and theirs gives about 1/16 mm error (8 mm gives 0.5 mm).
Mono PDs (bridge centre to each pupil centre) are needed for asymmetry, strabismus (occlude the other eye), progressives, aspherics and anisometropia.
Measure near centration distance (NCD) in the spectacle plane after fitting the frame, with the patient fixating a target at their working distance, not near PD in the facial plane.
A pupillometer uses the first Purkinje image, avoids parallax and gives binocular and mono PDs at set distances.

Multifocals: frame adjusted as worn, natural head posture, segment top usually at the lower limbus or lid (note an existing wearer's position, but ask if they're happy), trifocal top at the bottom of the pupil, measured from the HCL.
Progressives: pantoscopic angle 8–12°, dot each pupil centre while the patient looks at your opposite eye, remove and refit to check, measure heights and mono PDs with a rule or template.
BVD is required for powers over ±5.00 D (BS 2738-3), measured along the line of sight perpendicular to the spectacle front with zero pantoscopic tilt.
Free-form progressives also need BVD, pantoscopic angle and dihedral (wrap) angle.
examTraps: Measuring near PD in the facial plane instead of near CD in the lens plane: converging eyes are closer together at the lens.
Measuring BVD with the head tilted or off the optical axis.
Forgetting to occlude the other eye when measuring mono PDs for a small or alternating strabismus.
Measuring PD close up instead of at arm's length, which increases the parallax error.

diagram.description: Practitioner and patient facing each other at about 40 cm with a PD rule on the patient's nose. Step 1: practitioner closes their right eye; patient looks at the practitioner's left eye; zero aligned with the patient's right pupil centre. Step 2: practitioner closes their left eye and opens the right; patient looks at that eye; read the scale at the patient's left pupil centre.

goDeeper.heading: Sources of error measuring BVD with a ruler
goDeeper.body: Estimating where the back vertex is (hard with thick lenses or frames; measure to the front and subtract the centre thickness instead), not measuring along the optical axis, parallax, and dummy lenses with a different base curve from the glazed lenses. Distometers, gauges (e.g. the Varilux measuring gauge) and digital systems avoid most of these.

goDeeper.heading: Pantoscopic angle
goDeeper.body: The angle in the vertical plane between the lens's optical axis and the eye's visual axis in primary gaze. It keeps the centre-of-rotation distance, and so the BVD and effective power, constant as the eye looks down.

goDeeper.heading: Not in the slides: near PD rule of thumb
goDeeper.body: Near PD at about 40 cm is typically 3–4 mm less than distance PD, but measuring NCD in the lens plane is more accurate than estimating it.

checklist.title: Measuring distance PD with a PD rule
steps: Explain what you're about to do and why.
Sit at the same eye level as the patient, about 40 cm away.
Rest the rule on the bridge of the nose, scale facing you.
Close your right eye; ask the patient to look at your left eye.
Line up zero with the centre of the patient's right pupil (or temporal limbus).
Close your left eye and open your right; ask the patient to look at your right eye.
Read the scale at the centre of the patient's left pupil (or nasal limbus).
Repeat to check repeatability; take monocular readings from the bridge centre if needed.
Measure near PD with one eye in the midline at the working distance.
Record distance PD, near PD and monocular PDs clearly.

flashcards.front: Effectivity formula when moving a lens towards the eye
flashcards.back: Fc = F / (1 − dF), with d in metres.
Lower the optical centres about 1 mm for every 2° of tilt.

flashcards.front: Above what power does vertex distance become important?
flashcards.back: Roughly ±4.00 D and above.

flashcards.front: Why switch eyes for distance PD?
flashcards.back: So the patient's lines of sight are parallel, mimicking distance fixation.

flashcards.front: Three extra measurements for free-form progressives
flashcards.back: Back vertex distance, pantoscopic angle and dihedral (wrap) angle.
Keeps the centre-of-rotation distance (and so BVD and effective power) constant as the eye looks down.

flashcards.front: Sources of error measuring BVD with a ruler
flashcards.back: Estimating the back vertex (thick lenses or frames), not measuring along the optical axis, parallax, and dummy lenses with a different base curve.

options.feedback: That's the answer for moving the lens AWAY from the eye. Moving a plus lens closer needs more plus.
At this power a 4 mm change is clinically significant.
Check your units: d must be in metres (0.004 m).

mcq.explanation: Moving a plus lens towards the eye reduces its effective power, so you compensate with more plus: Fc = F / (1 − dF).

options.feedback: With tilt, OCs at the pupil mean the optical axis misses the centre of rotation.

options.feedback: That's 1 mm per degree; the rule is 1 mm per 2°.

mcq.q: Why measure PD at arm's length rather than close up?

options.text: It reduces the error from any difference between your PD and the patient's
options.feedback: Yes: about 1/16 mm per mm difference at 40 cm.

options.text: So the patient can't see the ruler

mcq.q: For which patient are mono PDs essential?

options.feedback: Yes, also for strabismus, aspherics, asymmetry and anisometropia.

options.text: A single vision wearer with a symmetrical face and a low Rx

mcq.q: Back vertex distance must be measured for powers over
How does a pupillometer avoid parallax?

options.text: It uses the first Purkinje image as the pupil reference
It measures each eye from the ear

mcq.q: Where is a general-purpose bifocal segment top usually fitted?

cases.scenario: A patient's distance PD reads 64 mm but the monocular PDs are R 30 / L 34. They've chosen varifocals.
cases.question: Which PD values do you send to the lab, and why?
cases.modelAnswer: Send the monocular PDs (R 30, L 34). Varifocal corridors are narrow, so each fitting cross must sit exactly in front of its own pupil. Splitting 64 into 32/32 would put the right corridor 2 mm temporal and the left 2 mm nasal, narrowing the clear intermediate and near zones.

cases.scenario: Worksheet 1, question 5: a patient with a small alternating strabismus.
cases.question: How would you measure their distance mono PDs with a ruler?
cases.modelAnswer: Face the patient square-on with your eyes level, at arm's length. Ruler zero at the centre of the bridge. Occlude their left eye and ask them to look at your left eye with their right eye; read to the centre of the right pupil. Then occlude the right eye, have them look at your right eye with their left, and read the left pupil. Occluding stops the deviating eye taking up fixation, which matters because with an alternating squint either eye may fixate.

cases.scenario: Worksheet answer example: R +2.00, L +5.00 with mono PDs of 30 and 33 mm, but glazed at 31.5 mm each.
cases.question: What prism does that induce?
cases.modelAnswer: Each lens is 1.5 mm out from its pupil. R: 0.15 cm × 2.00 = 0.3Δ base out. L: 0.15 cm × 5.00 = 0.75Δ base in. Both bases point the same way, so the differential is 0.75 − 0.3 = 0.45Δ base in: unlikely to bother orthophores or exophores, but it could tip an esophore into symptoms. Off-axis aberrations also increase when the patient isn't looking through the optical centres.

topics.title: Centration, decentration & Prentice's rule
topics.summary: Any point on a lens away from its optical centre has prism (Prentice's rule, P = cF with c in cm), and also more off-axis aberration. In the multifocal lectures this explains prism at the near vision point, image jump and the differential prism that anisometropes get when they look down.
keyPoints: Prentice's rule: P (Δ) = c (cm) × F (D). The optical centre is the point with no prism; every other point has prism and more off-axis aberration.
Use the power in the meridian you need: a cyl at axis 180 acts fully in the vertical meridian, a cyl at axis 90 not at all. For other axes Fθ = F sin²θ (not examined for prism).
Looking down through a plus lens gives base-up prism; through a minus lens, base-down. Looking in towards the nose gives base-out for plus and base-in for minus.
Differential prism: R −1.00 DS, L −6.00 DS, 8 mm below the optical centres gives 0.8Δ and 4.8Δ base-down, so 4Δ base-down in the left (or base-up in the right).
Vertical differential prism at near depends only on the distance portions when both segments match.
Fixes: prism-controlled bifocals, unequal segment sizes (differential = (r₂ − r₁) × add), bi-prism (slab-off) lenses, or free-form lenses.
Centring errors matter more with anisometropia: if one eye is decentred differently, the two prisms no longer cancel.
examTraps: Using millimetres instead of centimetres in Prentice's rule (a 10× error).
Including the cyl in the vertical meridian when its axis is 90, or leaving it out when its axis is 180.
Adding prisms with the same base direction instead of subtracting when working out differential prism, or vice versa: work out where each image moves.

diagram.description: Two lens cross-sections side by side. Left: plus lens drawn as two prisms base-to-base, with a ray passing 5 mm below the OC deviated upwards (base up). Right: minus lens drawn as two prisms apex-to-apex, with a ray 5 mm below the OC deviated downward (base down). Labels: OC, c (decentration), base direction.

goDeeper.heading: Worked example: decentration with anisometropia
goDeeper.body: From the facial measurement answers: R +2.00 and L +5.00 with mono PDs of 30 and 33 mm glazed at 31.5 mm each. Each lens is 1.5 mm out: R 0.15 × 2 = 0.3Δ base out, L 0.15 × 5 = 0.75Δ base in. Both bases point the same way, giving 0.45Δ base in, enough to upset an esophore.

goDeeper.heading: Not in the slides: decentration and blank size
goDeeper.body: Decentration per eye = (box centre distance − PD) ÷ 2, or half the box centre distance minus the mono PD.

options.feedback: BCD 70 − PD 64 = 6 mm total, 3 mm in per eye.
The frame centres are wider than the pupils, so the OCs move inwards.

mcq.q: R +3.00 D, L +3.00 D. Both OCs are placed 1.5 mm temporal of each pupil. What total horizontal prism results?

options.feedback: Each eye looks 0.15 cm nasal of a plus lens OC. Plus lens bases point towards the OC (temporal) → 0.45Δ base out each, 0.9Δ base out total.
Plus lens = base towards the OC. The OC is temporal, so the base is out.
Both eyes get base out, so it adds rather than cancels.

mcq.explanation: P = 0.15 × 3 = 0.45Δ per eye; same base direction relative to the face (both out), so they add.

options.feedback: Yes: 0.6 × 4 = 2.4; looking down through minus gives base down.
Base up comes with plus lenses below the OC.

options.feedback: Yes: a cyl at axis 90 has no power vertically.
That adds the cyl, which acts horizontally.

options.feedback: The prisms have the same base direction, so subtract.

Looking in towards the nose through a plus lens gives

options.feedback: Yes: plus lenses act base-to-base, base towards the OC.

cases.question: Calculate the vertical prism imbalance and suggest what could help.
cases.modelAnswer: R: 1.0 × 6 = 6Δ base down. L: 1.0 × 2 = 2Δ base down. Imbalance = 4Δ (R base down relative to L). Options: separate reading specs centred for near, slab-off (bi-prism) on the more minus lens, or contact lenses. Check with your lecturer which solutions the department expects you to discuss.

topics.title: Lens materials
topics.summary: Lens materials are compared by refractive index (higher = thinner), Abbe number (higher = less chromatic aberration), density (weight), impact resistance and UV absorption. CR39 is the standard plastic; polycarbonate and Trivex are the safety choices; high-index plastics suit stronger prescriptions.
keyPoints: Refractive index (n): higher index bends light more, so the lens can be thinner for the same power.
Abbe number (V): measures dispersion. Higher V means less colour fringing (transverse chromatic aberration) off-axis.
As index rises, Abbe number generally falls — the classic trade-off.
Reflectance per surface ≈ ((n − 1)/(n + 1))². For n = 1.5 that's about 4% per surface.
Typical values (check your slides): CR39 n ≈ 1.50, V ≈ 58; crown glass n ≈ 1.52, V ≈ 59; Trivex n ≈ 1.53, V ≈ 43–45; polycarbonate n ≈ 1.59, V ≈ 30; 1.67 plastic V ≈ 32.
Polycarbonate and Trivex: high impact resistance, recommended for children, sports and safety use.
Higher-index materials reflect more light, so anti-reflection coating matters more.
examTraps: Saying high index lenses are always lighter — thinner, yes, but density varies (high-index glass is heavy).
Recommending polycarbonate to someone very sensitive to colour fringing without mentioning the low Abbe number.
Forgetting that thickness savings matter most at the edge of minus lenses and the centre of plus lenses.

diagram.description: Scatter chart: x-axis refractive index (1.49–1.75), y-axis Abbe number (25–60). Points for CR39, crown glass, Trivex, polycarbonate, 1.60, 1.67, 1.74. Shows the downward trend.

goDeeper.heading: Why index affects thickness
goDeeper.body: Surface power F = (n − 1)/r. With a higher n you can achieve the same power with a flatter curve (bigger r), so the sag of the surface and hence the thickness difference between centre and edge shrinks.

goDeeper.heading: Abbe number in practice
goDeeper.body: Chromatic aberration is only noticeable when looking away from the optical centre, especially with strong prescriptions. A low-Abbe lens (e.g. polycarbonate) in a high prescription can give coloured fringes around objects in peripheral gaze. Accurate centration reduces the problem.

goDeeper.heading: Choosing a material for a patient
goDeeper.body: Think: power, frame size and type (rimless needs a tough material such as polycarbonate or Trivex to avoid cracking at drill holes), age and lifestyle (children → impact resistance), cosmetic concerns (thickness), and budget.

flashcards.front: What does a high Abbe number mean?
flashcards.back: Low dispersion — less chromatic aberration.

flashcards.front: Best material choice for a child's specs?
flashcards.back: Polycarbonate or Trivex, for impact resistance.
About 1.50 and 58.

mcq.q: Which material is best for a rimless (drilled) frame for an active 10-year-old?

options.feedback: Tough, impact resistant, resists cracking at drill holes and has a better Abbe number than polycarbonate.
Glass is heavy and can shatter, so it's unsuitable for children or drilled mounts.
CR39 can crack around drill holes and has lower impact resistance.
Not needed for most child prescriptions, and less impact resistant than Trivex or polycarbonate.

mcq.explanation: For children and drilled frames, impact resistance comes first: Trivex or polycarbonate.

mcq.q: Approximately what percentage of light is reflected from one surface of an uncoated lens with n = 1.6?

options.feedback: That's roughly both surfaces combined, not one.
That's closer to a coated surface.

mcq.explanation: R = ((n − 1)/(n + 1))². Higher-index lenses reflect more, so they benefit more from anti-reflection coating.

mcq.q: What does a higher refractive index allow?

options.text: A thinner lens for the same power

mcq.q: What does a high Abbe number (V) mean?

options.text: Low dispersion, so less colour fringing

mcq.q: Using ((n − 1)/(n + 1))², about how much light does a surface of n = 1.5 reflect?
Which material is usually recommended for children and sports?

options.feedback: Less impact-resistant than polycarbonate or Trivex.

mcq.q: Why does anti-reflection coating matter more for high-index lenses?

options.text: They reflect more light at each surface

mcq.q: Which has the lowest Abbe number of these?
Why dispense higher index only if it's genuinely thinner in the chosen frame?

options.text: Its lower V value adds transverse chromatic aberration
options.feedback: Yes, from the lens design lecture.

cases.scenario: A patient with R −7.50 / L −7.75 wants a large rectangular frame and hates thick edges.
cases.question: What would you advise on material and frame?
cases.modelAnswer: Suggest a high-index material (e.g. 1.67 or 1.74) with an anti-reflection coating, and explain the lower Abbe number. Gently recommend a smaller, rounder frame with a BCD close to their PD to reduce decentration and edge thickness; a thicker acetate rim can hide the edge. Aspheric design also helps.

topics.title: Lens form and lens design
topics.summary: With only two spherical surfaces, a lens designer can remove one off-axis aberration and reduce another. Week 8's lecture covers the best-form philosophies, field diagrams and Tscherning's ellipses, and how lens form and material affect what you dispense.
keyPoints: Aberrations that matter in spectacle design: oblique astigmatism, curvature of field, transverse chromatic aberration and distortion. Lens form makes no difference on-axis.
Curved form: one surface convex and the other concave in all meridians (BS EN ISO 13666).
Best form: curves chosen to eliminate or minimise a stated defect for a set object distance, centre of rotation distance and refractive index.
Point focal (zero OAE), Percival (zero MOE) and minimum tangential error (tangential power = BVP, the commonest modern choice).

Tscherning's ellipses give two solutions for each power between about −22 D and +7 D: the flatter Ostwalt form (used in practice) and the steeper Wollaston form. Outside that range you need aspheric surfaces.
TCA is controlled by choosing a high-V material; distortion is usually tolerated unless the form or Rx changes a lot.
Dispense best-form curved designs as standard; only use higher index if it's genuinely thinner for that frame, because lower V means more TCA.
examTraps: Assuming best form is best for everyone: a young myope may see better in a flatter lens because its negative MOE can be overcome by accommodating.
Changing a high-prescription wearer's lens form without warning: the change in distortion can cause complaints.

diagram.description: Light hitting a lens with a thin coating. Two reflected rays (from the air–coating and coating–lens boundaries) half a wavelength out of step, cancelling. Labels: incident light, coating (quarter-wave thickness), reflected rays cancel, transmitted light increases.

goDeeper.heading: −4.00 D: curved versus flat
goDeeper.body: The best-form curved lens (+5.00/−9.00) has almost no OAE and a small positive MOE (+0.36 D at 40°), too little minus at the edges, which a young wearer can't accommodate away. Plano-concave has much more OAE and a negative MOE (−1.01 D at 40°), which a non-presbyope can accommodate for, but distortion rises faster.

goDeeper.heading: Not in the slides: coatings and tints
goDeeper.body: Anti-reflection coatings use thin-film interference; hard coats provide scratch resistance (AR doesn't); photochromics darken less behind a UV-blocking windscreen; polarised lenses cut horizontally polarised glare but can black out some LCD screens. Coatings, filters, tints and polarised lenses are all part of occupational dispensing choices.

flashcards.front: Main benefit of an aspheric lens
flashcards.back: Flatter and thinner with less magnification change, while controlling off-axis errors.

flashcards.front: What does a polarised lens block?
flashcards.back: Horizontally polarised reflected glare (water, roads, snow).
Windscreens block much UV, so many photochromics darken less while driving.
Thin-film destructive interference between reflections.

mcq.q: A keen angler wants to see into the water better. What would you recommend?

options.feedback: They cut the horizontally polarised glare from the water's surface.
AR reduces reflections from the lens, not glare from the water.
They reduce brightness but don't remove polarised glare.

mcq.explanation: Reflected glare is horizontally polarised; vertically oriented polarising filters block it.

mcq.q: What makes a lens 'curved form'?

options.text: One surface convex and the other concave in all meridians

mcq.q: Which design philosophy gives zero mean oblique error?

options.feedback: That makes the tangential power equal the BVP.

topics.title: Bifocals and trifocals
topics.summary: Weeks 3 and 4: why presbyopes need an addition, how bifocals developed, segment types and terminology, fitting, measuring the add, trifocals, and the optical problems of bifocals (prism at the near vision point, jump, aberrations and differential prism) with the prism-controlled designs that fix them. Progressives have their own topic.
keyPoints: Addition = near Rx − distance Rx. Put both in the same cyl form before subtracting.
Commonest bifocal today: solid plastic front-surface D28. Available D28, D35 (D40 specialist), R22 to R45, C28.
Optical ranking best to worst: split, E-style, prism-controlled, shaped (D), round, fused, seamless. Cosmetically almost the reverse.
Segment choice depends on Rx (round better for plus, D better for minus), field, occupation, appearance, weight, material and previous lenses.

Segment top position is measured from the HCL; segment drop from the distance optical centre; geometric inset from the distance centration point. Fit the top at the lower limbus for general use and keep a happy wearer's height.
Measure the add on the surface that carries the segment: front vertex power for front-surface segments (all plastic and fused glass). Distance power is always back vertex power.
Trifocal intermediate add is usually 50–60% of the near add; fit its top at the bottom of the pupil.
Near vision point (where the wearer looks) and near optical centre (zero combined prism) rarely coincide: X = YA ÷ (F + A).
Round segments add base-down prism at the NVP: helpful for plus, unhelpful for minus. Jump = segment-top-to-centre distance (cm) × add; E-style and semicircular segments have none.
TCA in a solid bifocal = prism at the NVP ÷ V; about 0.1Δ is noticeable.
examTraps: Measuring a front-surface add with back vertex power: it over-reads, especially on thick steep lenses.

goDeeper.heading: Why older presbyopes need a trifocal

goDeeper.heading: Prism-controlled bifocals
goDeeper.body: Used to neutralise prism at the NVP, give base-in at near for exophoria or convergence insufficiency, remove differential prism, or avoid jump. Options: Franklin split, Presto (segment glued into a hole), extra inset (prism = (inset − convergence) × add), unequal segment sizes, and bi-prism (slab-off) lenses, which always give base-up at near and go on the eye with least plus or most minus.

cases.scenario: A 58-year-old accountant spends 8 hours a day on two monitors and drives home. Current specs are bifocals.
cases.question: What would you suggest, and how would you explain it?
cases.modelAnswer: A pair of occupational (office) lenses for work, giving wide intermediate for the monitors and near for paperwork, plus varifocals or keeping the bifocals for driving and general use. Explain that one lens can't give wide zones at all distances, and that office lenses aren't suitable for driving.

cases.scenario: Worksheet 2: Px J (R −7.00 DS, L −6.50 DS, add +3.00) had high-index D28 bifocals and wants a bigger reading area. The choice is a large round segment or an E-style.
cases.question: Compare the two, then work out the vertical prism at an NVP 12 mm below the distance optical centre with an R45 segment and a 6 mm segment drop.
cases.modelAnswer: Round: less visible dividing line, but its base-down prism at the NVP adds to the minus lens's base-down, increasing aberrations and TCA (made worse by high-index material's low V value), and it jumps. E-style: largest reading area, segment centre on the dividing line so base-up at the NVP reduces the distance prism and there is no jump, but the line is more obvious. Prism: NVP is 6 mm below the segment top, so c for the segment = 22.5 − 6 = 16.5 mm. Right: 7.00 × 1.2 = 8.4Δ + 3.00 × 1.65 = 4.95Δ = 13.35Δ base-down. Left: 6.50 × 1.2 = 7.8Δ + 4.95Δ = 12.75Δ base-down. Their old D28 (depth = radius = 14 mm) gave 1.8Δ base-up from the segment, so the R45 gives 6.75Δ more base-down.

cases.scenario: Worksheet 3: Px R wears +2.50/−0.50 × 180 in both eyes, add +2.50, R30 segment with its top 5 mm below the distance optical centre. NVP is 14 mm below the distance optical centre.
cases.question: Find the vertical prism at the NVP and the position of the near optical centre.
cases.modelAnswer: Vertical power = +2.00 D (cyl at 180 acts vertically). Distance: 2.00 × 1.4 = 2.8Δ base-up. The NVP is 9 mm below the segment top, so 6 mm above the segment centre: 2.50 × 0.6 = 1.5Δ base-down. Total 1.3Δ base-up. ON: Y = 5 + 15 = 20 mm, X = 2.0 × 2.50 ÷ 4.50 = 1.11 cm, so ON is 11.1 mm below the distance optical centre, about 3 mm above the NVP.

cases.scenario: Worksheet 8: Px P wears R +6.00/+2.00 × 180, L +6.00/−2.00 × 180, add +2.00, in R22 bifocals, and prefers single-vision readers because the bifocals are tiring to read with.
cases.question: Explain why, calculate the vertical differential prism 12 mm below the distance optical centre, and say how you could fix it.
cases.modelAnswer: The prescriptions look alike but one is in plus cyl and one in minus: vertical power R +8.00, L +4.00. Through readers they look through the optical centres, so there is no induced prism. In the bifocals: R 9.6Δ base-up, L 4.8Δ base-up, a difference of 4.8Δ base-up in the right (the matched segments cancel out). Fix with prism control, e.g. 4.8Δ base-up in the left at near with a bi-prism or Presto bifocal. Unequal segments would need r₂ = 4.8 ÷ 2 + 1.1 = 3.5 cm, a 70 mm segment in the right, which isn't generally available.

cases.scenario: Worksheet 6: Dr L (46), a university lecturer who reads for a hobby, has R −1.50/−0.25 × 90, L −1.00/−0.50 × 95, add +1.25. They insist on bifocals because their partner had trouble with varifocals.
cases.question: Which segment would you discuss, and will screen work be a problem?
cases.modelAnswer: D28 is the commonest: more visible than a round segment, but for minus lenses its base-up at the NVP offsets the distance base-down. Round: less visible, more reading area, but adds base-down prism and more jump. E-style: largest reading area and no jump, but the most visible line. With a +1.25 add they can still see to about 80 cm through the segment, and their uncorrected far points (about 62 cm R and 80 cm L) mean they may see the screen without correction anyway; through the segment they may need to tilt their head back.

topics.title: Verification, transposition & fitting
topics.summary: Before glasses go to the patient they're checked against the prescription and order: powers and axes on the focimeter, optical centres or fitting points, prism, segment heights and physical condition, against BS EN ISO tolerances. Then the frame is adjusted on the face so it sits as measured.
keyPoints: Transposition: add the sphere and cyl for the new sphere, change the cyl sign, rotate the axis by 90°.
Focimeter: focus eyepiece first, check zero, measure back vertex power with the lens back surface against the stop.
Mark the optical centres with the focimeter and check centration and any prism against the order.
Varifocals are verified at the distance and near reference points — not at the fitting cross.
Check against tolerances from BS EN ISO 21987 (mounted lenses) — learn the version on your slides.
Fitting: the frame should be level, sit at the measured vertex distance, have even pressure behind the ears and correct pantoscopic tilt.

Checking a varifocal's power at the fitting cross.

Place spectacles back surface towards the stop, lens table touching both lower rims so axes are referenced to the frame's horizontal. Find the first line focus, read sphere and axis, then the second line for the cyl. Centre the target and mark the OC.

goDeeper.heading: Collection and fitting

Heat acetate frames gently; adjust metal frames with the correct pliers. Ask the patient to look down and shake their head gently to check stability.

topics.title: Progressive power lenses
topics.summary: Progressives give continuous focus from distance to near through a corridor of steadily increasing power, at the cost of unwanted astigmatism at the sides. Design, add and corridor length decide how wide the clear zones are; good fitting decides whether the patient copes.
keyPoints: Three zones: distance at the top, a progression corridor, near at the bottom. Conventional PPLs carry the progression on the front surface.
Two main design factors: the progression formula, and the way tangential and sagittal powers are matched along the meridian line, which pushes astigmatism into the periphery.
Surface astigmatism grows with a higher add and a shorter corridor, narrowing intermediate and near zones. The corridor of clear vision is where astigmatism is under 1.00 D.
Linear progression: add at a point = rate × distance below the prism checking point. Power there = distance power in that meridian + add; prism = F × c.
Short-corridor lenses fit about 14 mm deep frames (standard about 18 mm) but have more astigmatism, so they suit low adds better.
Occupational lenses use a small degression (about −0.75 to −1.25 D) from near to intermediate, so they have wide, easy zones but often no proper distance.
Prism thinning: equal base-down prism in both lenses to balance edge thickness. A difference in vertical prism between the eyes at the prism checking point is prescribed prism.
examTraps: Calling prism thinning a way to make lenses thinner overall. It only balances top and bottom edge thickness.
Recommending a short corridor for a high add.
Comparing iso-cylinder plots from different manufacturers as if they were measured the same way.

goDeeper.heading: Where the swimming feeling comes from
goDeeper.body: Looking sideways, the astigmatism changes at different rates in the two lenses, so magnification differs between the eyes. The brain sees the two images moving at different speeds and in slightly different directions. It is worse with higher adds, so starting people in progressives while their add is low helps. Free-form designs can match the right and left astigmatism to reduce it.

goDeeper.heading: Free-form versus conventional
goDeeper.body: Conventional: one formula cut into a front-surface semi-finished blank, the same design across a range of prescriptions, needing only monocular PDs and heights. Free-form: point-by-point surfaces, often on the back, tailored to the prescription, working distances and frame fit, needing BVD, pantoscopic tilt, wrap and near working distance. They can also control differential prism and magnification.

goDeeper.heading: Dispensing checklist
goDeeper.body: Adjust the frame first and check the depth suits the design. Face the patient at the same eye level in their natural head posture; they look at your left eye while you mark their right pupil, and vice versa. Remove the frame, replace it and recheck the marks. Verify by re-marking from the engravings with the correct template.

Hobbies: car restoration may mean looking up close in awkward positions; snooker needs intermediate high in the lens or the head tilts back; golf needs a clear ball below, which the near zone may blur. topics.title: Aberrations of spectacle lenses
topics.summary: Why real lenses don't form perfect images, which aberrations matter for spectacles (mainly oblique astigmatism and transverse chromatic aberration), and how to calculate them.
keyPoints: First-order (paraxial) optics: sin i = i for angles up to about 5°; always predicts a perfect image.
Third-order (Seidel) optics adds the i³/3! term and is reasonably accurate to about 20°. It gives five aberrations: spherical aberration, coma, oblique astigmatism, curvature of field and distortion.
Spherical aberration and coma are ignored in spectacle lens design: the pupil limits them and the eye has more of its own.
Oblique astigmatism is the most important; it is controlled with best-form or aspheric lenses.
Vertex sphere: centred on the eye's centre of rotation, through the lens back vertex. Far point sphere: the far point as the eye rotates, one back vertex focal length beyond.
OAE = FT − FS; MOP = (FT + FS) ÷ 2; MOE = MOP − F′v.
TCA = prism ÷ V = F × c ÷ V (Δ, with c in cm); about 0.1Δ is the threshold. High-index materials have low V and so more TCA.

Best-form lens: a spherical lens with curves chosen to eliminate or minimise a stated defect under defined conditions (object distance, centre of rotation distance, refractive index). Lens form makes no difference on-axis.
Three design philosophies: point focal (zero OAE), Percival (zero MOE, so MOP = BVP), and minimum tangential error (tangential power = BVP), the commonest modern choice.
Tscherning's ellipses: two solutions for each power, the flatter Ostwalt (used in practice) and the steeper Wollaston, for powers from about −22 D to +7 D only.
examTraps: Measuring tangential and sagittal focal lengths from the lens instead of from the vertex sphere.
Mixing up dispersive power and V: V = 1 ÷ dispersive power.
Saying lens designers correct spherical aberration. They concentrate on oblique astigmatism.
Thinking a best-form lens is best for everyone: a young myope may see better with a flatter lens because its negative MOE can be overcome by accommodating.
Dispensing higher index without checking that it's actually thinner in that frame; it always adds TCA.

goDeeper.heading: Distortion and lens form
goDeeper.body: Minus lenses give barrel distortion (magnification falls off-axis) and plus lenses pincushion. The brain adapts to a lens it is used to, so problems arise when a high-prescription wearer changes lens form. Some myopes prefer flatter lenses even though their off-axis performance is worse.

goDeeper.heading: Diffraction-limited images
goDeeper.body: An image with no aberrations is still not a perfect point: the limiting aperture (the pupil, in the eye) diffracts light into a small disc. The smaller the aperture, the bigger the effect, but in practice aberrations usually mask it.

flashcards.back: Spherical aberration, coma, oblique astigmatism, curvature of field, distortion.

flashcards.back: Oblique astigmatism.
Barrel: points displaced towards the axis (minus lenses). Pincushion: displaced away (plus lenses).
F ÷ V (dioptres). Not usually a concern because the eye's own LCA masks it.

cases.scenario: Worksheet 2: a +200 mm lens sits 25 mm in front of the centre of rotation. At 30° off axis the sagittal focus is 193 mm and the tangential focus 196 mm from the lens along the principal ray; the vertex sphere is 3 mm from the lens along that ray.
cases.question: Find the OAE, MOP and MOE.
cases.modelAnswer: Measure from the vertex sphere: fS = 190 mm, fT = 193 mm. FS = +5.26 D, FT = +5.18 D. OAE = FT − FS = −0.08 D. MOP = (5.18 + 5.26) ÷ 2 = +5.22 D. MOE = 5.22 − 5.00 = +0.22 D: slightly more plus than wanted off-axis.

cases.scenario: Worksheet 4: Px B (R −7.50/−0.75 × 25, L −6.50/−1.00 × 165) collects new spectacles and says vision isn't as good. VA equals the old pair, the Rx is right and the centration matches their PD.
cases.question: What could be wrong, how would you check, and what would you do?
cases.modelAnswer: Probably a change in lens form, changing the distortion (and off-axis performance) they were used to. Compare the surface curves of old and new lenses with a lens measure. Explain the design is different and the brain usually adapts; ask them to wear the new pair for about two weeks without switching back, and return if no better. If they still can't adapt, remake in a form closer to the old lenses (some myopes prefer flatter forms).

cases.scenario: Worksheet 3: a lens designed for zero tangential error, BVP −2.50 D. At 40° the sagittal focal length from the back surface is −330 mm; the vertex sphere is 12 mm from the lens.
cases.question: Find the OAE, MOP and MOE.
cases.modelAnswer: From the vertex sphere: fS = −330 − 12 = −342 mm, so FS = −2.924 D. Zero tangential error means FT = BVP = −2.50 D. OAE = −2.50 − (−2.924) = +0.42 D. MOP = (−2.50 − 2.924) ÷ 2 = −2.71 D. MOE = −2.71 − (−2.50) = −0.21 D.

cases.scenario: Worksheet 5: Px B, R +6.50 DS, L +7.00 DS, wants the cheapest possible spectacles.
cases.question: How can you keep the lenses thin without paying more than for standard lenses, and what compromises might you need?
cases.modelAnswer: Frame: small eye size, a round shape (spherical Rx), plastic (thinner minimum edge), and a CD matching the PD to minimise decentration and blank size. Lenses: aspheric would be ideal but costs more; a semi-finished lens surfaced to minimum edge thickness may be thinner than a stock lens whose blank is bigger than needed, for a small extra cost. Best form needs steep plus curves (thick), so a flatter form would be thinner but blurrier off-axis; discuss that trade-off with the patient.

cases.scenario: Worksheet 4: a −15.00 D back surface on a Tscherning's ellipse for a Percival design.
cases.question: Which two BVPs does it suit, why not use it for the more positive one, and what is better?
cases.modelAnswer: About −14.50 D and +4.00 D. For +4.00 D the front would need to be +19.00 D, a very bulbous lens. The flatter Ostwalt solution, about +11.00/−7.00, is the better choice.

topics.title: Aspheric lenses
topics.summary: Aspheric surfaces flatten (or steepen) away from the optical axis. That built-in surface astigmatism can cancel oblique astigmatism, allowing high plus lenses with good off-axis vision and flatter, thinner low-power lenses.
keyPoints: An aspheric ophthalmic surface is non-spherical but rotationally symmetrical about its axis; toric and progressive surfaces don't qualify.
Spherical best-form solutions don't exist above about +7.00 D, so aspherics were first used for high plus (aphakia).
Conic p values: circle 1, prolate ellipse between 0 and 1, parabola 0, hyperbola below 0, oblate ellipse above 1. The smaller p, the more the surface flattens.
Sag: x = y² ÷ [r₀ + √(r₀² − py²)]. Thickness: tc + S2 = te + S1.
Surface radii away from the axis: rs = √[r₀² + (1 − p)y²], rt = rs³ ÷ r₀².
Low powers: an aspheric front allows a flatter form with best-form optics; combined with high index it saves thickness twice over.
Dispensing: centre accurately, don't decentre to make prism, and use atoroidal surfaces for higher cylinders.
examTraps: Calling a toric or progressive surface aspheric.
Mixing up the order of n′ and n when working out r₀ for a back surface.
Assuming an aspheric designed for a sphere works for a big cylinder: the ideal p differs between meridians.

goDeeper.heading: Choosing the p value
goDeeper.body: For a +10.00 D lens at 35°: p = 1 (sphere) gives OAE 2.29 D and MOE +1.27 D; p = 0.4 gives MOE about 0 (Percival-like) with OAE 0.89; p = 0 gives OAE 0.15 with MOE −0.65 (point focal-like, and a young wearer can accommodate for negative MOE); p = −4 overcorrects badly. So p 0.4 suits presbyopes and p 0 suits non-presbyopes.

goDeeper.heading: Verifying an aspheric
goDeeper.body: Move a lens measure from the centre outwards. A spherical surface reads the same everywhere; an aspheric plus front reads less towards the edge, and on a minus lens the power increases towards the edge.

cases.scenario: Worksheet 5: Px H (R +10.50 DS, L +10.75/−0.75 × 45) wanted a cheap second pair. You made spherical-front lenses surfaced to the Rx in a carefully chosen frame. They complain the edges are blurred, though their first pair is clear.
cases.question: Why, and what would you do?
cases.modelAnswer: No spherical best form exists above about +7.00 D, so the spherical lens has a lot of oblique astigmatism and mean oblique error off-axis. The first pair was almost certainly aspheric (and perhaps flatter), with its asphericity chosen to cancel those errors. Check the first pair's surfaces with a lens measure (power falling towards the edge suggests aspheric) and remake the new pair with aspheric fronts, centred accurately.

topics.title: Occupational and recreational dispensing
topics.summary: Matching spectacles to the job: analyse the task, check the worker meets any visual standards, and protect the eyes from hazards at work and play.
keyPoints: Visibility (task: size, distance, lighting, contrast, colour, time, movement, glare) versus visual capability (worker: VA, fields, binocular vision, colour, depth, adaptation).
For sustained tasks, VA should be about twice as good as the minimum needed; use a nomogram to find it from detail size and distance.
Group 1 driving: number plate at 20 m, 6/12 binocular, 120° horizontal field (50° each side) with no significant central defect. Group 2: 6/7.5 better eye, 6/60 worse, spectacles within ±8 D.
Regular VDU users (an hour or more continuously each day) are entitled to an eye exam from the employer, who pays for basic spectacles if needed only for VDU work.
Employers assess risk and supply PPE; practices can adjust but not repair safety eyewear.
Chemical injury is the most urgent eye emergency: irrigate, don't pad, refer immediately.
examTraps: Thinking 6/12 alone satisfies the driving standard: the number plate test and fields must also be met (6/7.5 practically guarantees the plate test).
Forgetting that standards usually exclude diplopia rather than phorias.

goDeeper.heading: Police and pilot standards
goDeeper.body: Police (GOV.UK): corrected 6/12 each eye and 6/6 binocularly, near 6/9, uncorrected 6/36, low-contrast 6/12, field 120° by 100°; monochromats rejected. Pilots: 6/6 binocular, 6/9 each eye, no anisometropia or astigmatism above 2.00 D, plus colour standards. Standards change, so always check the current version.

flashcards.back: 6/9 better eye, 6/12 other, N8 near, no colour deficiency.
Welding flash (arc eye, a UV photokeratitis).
Distracting, discomforting and disabling.

cases.question: Which visual criteria matter for a crane driver, an electrician, a table tennis player and an accountant?
cases.modelAnswer: Crane driver: depth perception and good peripheral fields. Electrician: reasonable VA and good colour vision (wiring colours). Table tennis player: depth perception, binocular status and eye movements. Accountant: reasonable intermediate and near VA for screens and paperwork.
